newsitem.title: USA: Vitamin E could help U.S. beef exports - study.
newsitem.headline: Vitamin E could help U.S. beef exports - study.

text.p: U.S. beef exports could be boosted and domestic prices cut if cattle were fed vitamin E supplements, according to the results of a study released on Wednesday.

The study found the supplements could reduce domestic retail losses due to discoloration to 13.6 percent, compared with 19.5 percent in unsupplemented beef. This could lead to a drop in retail prices as the losses are factored into current prices, said Brad Morgan, an animal scientist at Oklahoma State University.

Morgan said it would also help U.S. beef exports compete with Australian beef in markets such as Japan. Australian beef is known for having a longer shelf life as it is naturally rich in Vitamin E as cattle are fed on grass for a prolonged period.
"U.S. beef from vitamin E supplemented cattle had vitamin E concentrations similar to Australian beef, eliminating Australian beef's competitive advantage," the study claimed.
Morgan said the U.S. had recently passed Australia as the leading exporter of beef to Japan and a longer shelf life would further improve its competitiveness.
Japan bought 545,000 tonnes of U.S. beef and beef-variety meats in 1996 out of total U.S. exports of 982,000 tonnes, according to figures issued this month by the U.S. Meat Export Federation.
The results will be presented to packers at a meeting of the American Meat Institute in Nashville in April, he said.

Retailers, packers and cattle feeders would have to work together to formulate premiums for cattle supplemented with vitamin E if the supplements are to be introduced, said Mike Engler of Cactus Feeders.
Engler estimated he would need an additional $3.50 a head to justify the supplements. The study estimated the overall advantage at $25.99 per carcass as boxed beef and $34.45 at the retail level.
The study was funded by the U.S. beef checkoff program and involved three feedyards, three packers, four U.S. supermarket chains and three Japanese stores.
Researchers from Oklahoma State University, Colorado State University and the University of Wisconsin helped to monitor results.
